question: State what FCA stands for.

points: Financial Conduct Authority (1)

question: Give two functions of the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA).

points: Regulates financial firms to ensure they treat customers fairly (1)
Protects consumers from mis-selling and financial crime (1)
Authorises and supervises financial firms operating in the UK (1)
Investigates financial misconduct and can impose fines or remove licences (1)

question: State what the Financial Ombudsman Service (FOS) does.

points: Independently resolves / investigates disputes between consumers and financial firms (1)
mark_scheme.additional_guidance: Accept any reasonable description of independent dispute resolution.

question: State two features of the Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS).

points: Protects deposits up to £85,000 per person per authorised institution if the institution fails (1)
Free to consumers — the cost is borne by the financial services industry (1)
Also covers investments, insurance and mortgage advice (1)

question: Identify the maximum amount protected by the FSCS for bank deposits.

points: £85,000 per person per authorised institution (1)

question: State one way a rise in the Bank of England base rate affects personal borrowers.

points: Monthly repayments on variable-rate loans and mortgages increase (1)
It becomes more expensive to take out new credit/borrowing (1)

question: Give two effects of high inflation on personal finances.

points: Purchasing power of savings is eroded — money buys less (1)
Real wages fall if pay rises do not keep pace with inflation (1)
Interest rates may rise to combat inflation, increasing borrowing costs (1)
Cost of everyday goods and services increases (1)

question: Identify two types of financial firms regulated by the FCA.

points: Banks (1)
Insurance companies (1)
Investment firms / stockbrokers (1)
Mortgage lenders / advisers (1)
Payday lenders (1)
Pension providers (1)

question: Give two features of the Financial Ombudsman Service.

points: Independent of financial firms and the government (1)
Free to consumers (1)
Can award up to £375,000 compensation to an individual (1)
Consumers must have complained to the firm first before approaching the FOS (1)

question: State two services provided by MoneyHelper (formerly the Money Advice Service).

points: Free, impartial money and debt advice (1)
Online guides and tools (e.g. budget planners, mortgage calculators) (1)
Signposts to other free debt and financial guidance services (1)
Pension wise service for those approaching retirement (1)

question: Give two ways in which taxation affects personal finances.

points: Income tax reduces take-home pay (1)
National Insurance contributions are deducted from earnings (1)
Inheritance tax may reduce the estate passed on to family (1)
Capital gains tax on profits from selling assets (1)
Council tax adds to cost of living (1)

question: Identify two state benefits available to individuals in the UK that affect personal finance.

points: Universal Credit (1)
State Pension (1)
Child Benefit (1)
Housing Benefit (1)
Personal Independence Payment (PIP) (1)

question: State two rights a consumer has under consumer credit regulation in the UK.

points: Right to a cooling-off period (e.g. 14 days for most credit agreements) (1)
Right to receive a pre-contractual credit agreement showing total cost (1)
Right to early repayment with a reduced interest charge (1)
Section 75 protection — credit card company jointly liable for purchases £100–£30,000 (1)

question: Give two ways a fall in the Bank of England base rate benefits consumers.

points: Mortgage and loan repayments decrease (1)
Cheaper to borrow money on credit cards and overdrafts (1)
Businesses may invest more and create jobs (1)

question: State two powers the FCA has when dealing with firms that break the rules.

points: Issue fines / financial penalties (1)
Withdraw or suspend a firm's authorisation / licence to operate (1)
Require the firm to pay redress / compensation to affected customers (1)
Prosecute individuals for financial crime (1)

scenario: QuickLend is an online short-term lender that has been charging consumers undisclosed fees and not explaining the true cost of credit.
question: Explain one action the FCA could take against QuickLend.

points: The FCA could issue a fine against QuickLend (1) to punish the firm for treating customers unfairly and to deter other firms from similar behaviour (1)
The FCA could revoke QuickLend's authorisation to operate (1) preventing it from continuing to harm consumers (1)
The FCA could require QuickLend to pay redress to affected customers (1) compensating them for undisclosed fees they were charged (1)

scenario: Priya took out a travel insurance policy and made a claim when her holiday was cancelled due to illness. The insurer refused to pay and Priya believes it is wrong to do so.
question: Explain the steps Priya should take using the FOS to resolve her complaint.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each step. Maximum 4 marks for two steps.
points: Priya must first formally complain to the insurer (1) and give the firm 8 weeks to respond with a final decision (1)

If the insurer rejects the complaint or does not respond within 8 weeks, Priya can take her case to the FOS (1) who will investigate independently and, if they agree with Priya, can direct the insurer to pay compensation (1)

scenario: Marcus has £200,000 in savings. He holds £90,000 at SunnyBank and £110,000 at another branch of the same organisation, SunnyBank Direct.
question: Explain what would happen to Marcus's savings if SunnyBank and SunnyBank Direct both failed simultaneously.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each point. Maximum 4 marks.
points: The FSCS covers up to £85,000 per person per authorised institution (1); if SunnyBank and SunnyBank Direct operate under the same banking licence/authorisation, Marcus is only covered up to £85,000 in total across both accounts (1)
This means Marcus's total £200,000 is only protected up to £85,000 (1) and he could lose up to £115,000 of his savings (1)
He should have spread his savings across institutions with different authorisations (1) to benefit from £85,000 FSCS protection at each (1)
mark_scheme.additional_guidance: Award up to 4 marks for a clear explanation of the risk and the implication for Marcus.

scenario: The Bank of England raised its base rate from 0.5% to 5% over 18 months to tackle inflation.
question: Explain two effects of this interest rate rise on personal finances.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each effect. Maximum 4 marks.
points: Mortgage repayments on tracker and variable-rate mortgages increased (1) reducing disposable income for affected homeowners (1)
Savings rates improved (1) allowing savers to earn more interest on deposits (1)
Cost of personal loans and credit card debt increased (1) making it more expensive for consumers to borrow (1)

scenario: Simone bought a laptop for £600 using her credit card. The laptop was faulty and the retailer has gone into administration.
question: Explain how Section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act protects Simone.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each point. Maximum 4 marks.
points: Section 75 makes the credit card company jointly liable with the retailer for purchases between £100 and £30,000 (1) so even though the retailer has failed, Simone can claim a refund from her credit card provider (1)
The laptop at £600 falls within the £100–£30,000 range (1) so Simone can make a claim directly to her credit card company for the cost of the faulty laptop (1)

scenario: The government has increased Universal Credit payments by 6%.
question: Explain one way this increase in Universal Credit may improve the personal finances of recipients.

points: Recipients receive a higher monthly income (1) which helps them meet essential expenditure such as rent, food, and utilities without going into debt (1)

scenario: PensionSure has been selling pension products to customers without properly explaining the risks, leaving many consumers with inappropriate products.
question: Explain how the FCA's role protects consumers in this situation.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each point. Maximum 4 marks.
points: The FCA can investigate PensionSure and assess whether it has met its regulatory obligations to treat customers fairly and provide clear information (1); if it finds misconduct it can require PensionSure to compensate affected customers (1)
The FCA can impose significant fines on PensionSure (1) deterring the firm and others from similar mis-selling practices in future (1)
The FCA can require PensionSure to contact all affected customers to explain their options and offer appropriate redress (1) restoring consumer confidence in the financial sector (1)

scenario: Ahmed has significant credit card debt and does not know where to turn for advice.
question: Explain how MoneyHelper could help Ahmed manage his debt situation.

points: MoneyHelper provides free, impartial debt advice (1) helping Ahmed understand his options such as a debt management plan, Individual Voluntary Arrangement (IVA) or bankruptcy without the cost of a paid financial adviser (1)

scenario: The UK experienced inflation of 11% in 2022–23. Many workers were on pay freezes.
question: Explain two ways this level of inflation could harm personal finances.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each way. Maximum 4 marks.
points: Workers on a pay freeze experienced a real-terms pay cut (1) as their income bought progressively less as prices rose by 11% (1)
The real value of savings eroded (1) as interest rates on many accounts were below 11%, meaning the purchasing power of savings fell (1)
Cost of essentials such as food, energy and transport increased sharply (1) reducing disposable income and forcing some households into debt (1)

scenario: Tariq was sold payment protection insurance (PPI) alongside his bank loan in 2008 without being properly informed it was optional.
question: Explain two ways consumer protection legislation and regulation could help Tariq recover compensation.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each way. Maximum 4 marks.
points: Tariq could make a formal complaint to the bank citing consumer credit regulations and the FCA's rules on treating customers fairly (1); if the bank rejects his complaint he can take it to the FOS, which has the power to direct the bank to compensate him (1)
The FCA-led PPI scheme created a process for claiming redress (1) and Tariq could have been entitled to the premium payments plus interest if he submitted a claim (1)

question: Explain why consumers must complain to their financial provider before contacting the FOS.

points: The firm is given the opportunity to resolve the complaint first (1) which may be faster and cheaper for both the consumer and the FOS than a formal investigation (1)
The FOS requires evidence that the firm has been given a fair chance to respond (1) and will not accept a complaint until the firm has issued a final response or 8 weeks have passed (1)

scenario: The UK government increased income tax thresholds, raising the personal allowance from £12,000 to £13,500.
question: Explain two ways this change in personal allowance benefits lower-income workers.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each benefit. Maximum 4 marks.
points: Lower-income workers earning below £13,500 will pay no income tax (1) increasing their net take-home pay (1)
Those earning just above the new threshold will pay less income tax overall (1) improving their disposable income for spending or saving (1)

scenario: Nadia has £120,000 in savings at one bank that is about to collapse.
question: Explain how Nadia should have managed her savings to ensure full FSCS protection.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each point. Maximum 4 marks.
points: Nadia should have split her savings across at least two differently authorised institutions (1) keeping no more than £85,000 at any single institution to maximise FSCS protection (1)
For example, she could hold £85,000 at one bank and £35,000 at a different bank (1) ensuring the full £120,000 is protected (1)

scenario: A payday lender is advertising a loan with an APR of 1,294%. The advert focuses on how quickly the cash is available but does not prominently display the APR.
question: Explain two ways the FCA could act to protect consumers from this advertising.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each action. Maximum 4 marks.
points: The FCA can require lenders to display the APR prominently in all advertising (1) so consumers can clearly see the true cost of borrowing before making a decision (1)
The FCA can investigate whether the advert is misleading (1) and order it to be withdrawn or amended to ensure it is fair, clear and not misleading (1)
The FCA can impose a fine on the lender (1) as a deterrent against producing non-compliant advertising in future (1)

scenario: The government has introduced a new 'Consumer Duty' requiring all regulated firms to demonstrate they are delivering good outcomes for customers.
question: Explain two ways the Consumer Duty could benefit personal consumers when dealing with financial firms.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each benefit. Maximum 4 marks.
points: Firms must ensure products are suitable for their target market (1) reducing the risk of consumers being sold inappropriate products such as high-risk investments to risk-averse individuals (1)
Firms must communicate in a clear and understandable way (1) helping consumers make informed financial decisions rather than being misled by complex jargon (1)
Firms must charge fair prices in relation to the value delivered (1) reducing the risk of consumers being overcharged for financial products (1)

scenario: The FCA has proposed capping the interest rate on all short-term consumer credit products at 100% of the original loan value (i.e. you can never repay more than twice what you borrowed).
question: Discuss the likely impact of this interest rate cap on consumers and lenders. (6)

indicative_content: Benefit to consumers: limits maximum repayable — prevents debt spirals from compounding interest
Benefit to vulnerable consumers: protects those in financial difficulty from catastrophic debts
Risk: some lenders may exit the market or tighten criteria, reducing credit availability
Those with poor credit ratings may lose access to credit entirely — could push them to illegal lenders
Lenders: reduced profitability, especially on long-defaulting loans; may increase upfront fees to compensate
Broader benefit: improved consumer confidence in the regulated lending market
Balanced conclusion: protects most consumers but may restrict credit access for the most vulnerable

level_descriptors.descriptor: Basic description of the cap; limited analysis.
Considers impact on both consumers and lenders; some development.
Well-developed, balanced discussion; addresses unintended consequences; justified conclusion.

scenario: Eloise had £95,000 in a savings account at EliteBank when it was declared insolvent. She is wondering whether she has lost money.
question: Discuss the extent to which Eloise is protected by the FSCS and what steps she should take. (6)

indicative_content: FSCS covers up to £85,000 per authorised institution — Eloise has £95,000
She will recover £85,000 from FSCS; the remaining £10,000 is unprotected
FSCS aims to compensate within 7 days for most bank failures
She should register her claim with the FSCS as soon as possible
She may need to join a creditor queue for the unprotected £10,000 — likely partial recovery only
She should have split savings to avoid this — lesson for future
Balanced conclusion: largely protected but £10,000 at risk — prompt action important

level_descriptors.descriptor: States the £85,000 limit; minimal analysis of her specific situation.
Calculates protected and unprotected amounts; advises some steps.
Well-developed; quantifies shortfall, explains FSCS process, advises on steps and lessons; justified conclusion.

scenario: The Bank of England is considering raising interest rates to 6% to control inflation of 9%. Many UK households have variable-rate mortgages.
question: Discuss the impact of this interest rate rise on UK households. (6)

indicative_content: Variable-rate mortgage holders: repayments increase — could cause financial hardship
Fixed-rate mortgage holders: not immediately affected until fixed period ends
Savers: benefit from higher rates on deposits
Borrowers with credit cards and loans: higher cost of existing variable-rate debt
Risk of mortgage arrears and repossessions for stretched households
Positive: brings inflation down over time, protecting purchasing power
Young people and first-time buyers: harder to afford mortgages
Balanced conclusion: significant short-term pain for mortgage borrowers; helps savers; may prevent worse long-term inflation damage

level_descriptors.descriptor: Generic statement about rates rising; limited context.
Identifies different groups affected; some development of impact.
Well-developed, balanced discussion covering borrowers, savers, fixed vs variable rates; justified conclusion.

scenario: The FCA has proposed that all regulated financial firms should offer customers a 'switching bonus' — a cash payment for moving to a competitor — to increase competition.
question: Discuss whether this proposal would benefit consumers. (6)

indicative_content: Benefit: incentivises consumers to shop around, potentially securing better rates/products
Increased competition could drive down prices and improve service quality
Risk: switching bonuses raise costs for firms, which may be passed on as higher fees
Some consumers may switch frequently for bonuses without considering the best long-term deal
Switching could be complex and off-putting without further simplification
Vulnerable/less financially engaged consumers may not benefit as much
Balanced conclusion: likely benefits engaged consumers; limited benefit for disengaged; unintended costs possible

level_descriptors.descriptor: Basic statement about switching being good; little analysis.
Identifies benefits and risks for consumers; some development.
Well-developed, balanced discussion; differentiates between consumer types; considers unintended consequences; justified conclusion.

scenario: The UK government is considering removing the Personal Savings Allowance and taxing all savings interest at the individual's marginal income tax rate.
question: Discuss the likely impact of this policy change on personal savers. (6)

indicative_content: Current PSA: basic rate taxpayers earn £1,000 interest tax-free; higher rate £500
If removed: savers pay income tax on all interest — higher earners pay more tax on savings
Impact on low earners: minimal if they remain within the old PSA limit anyway — now taxed
Impact on significant savers: meaningful reduction in net returns, incentive to use ISAs
ISA usage likely to increase — more demand for ISA products
May discourage saving — particularly for those near the old PSA threshold
Government revenue rises — might fund public services
Balanced conclusion: negative for most savers; disproportionate impact on middle-income savers; ISAs become more important

level_descriptors.descriptor: Basic description of the change; minimal analysis.
Identifies different groups affected; some development of impact on saving behaviour.
Thorough, balanced discussion; considers tax impact by income band, ISA switch, saving incentives; justified conclusion.

scenario: In 2020, StellarMortgages was found by the FCA to have sold inappropriate interest-only mortgages to 8,500 customers, many of whom are now unable to repay the capital at the end of the term. [Table: Customers affected: 8,500; Average shortfall at end of term: £45,000; Customers who complained: 1,200; FOS uphold rate: 78%; StellarMortgages annual profit: £22m; FCA maximum fine: 10% of global turnover; FSCS protection on mortgages: none for advice given in good faith]
question: Evaluate how effectively the regulatory and consumer protection framework protects the affected customers. (12)

indicative_content: FCA can fine StellarMortgages and require redress — strong deterrent; fine could be significant relative to £22m profit
FOS 78% uphold rate means most of the 1,200 complainants likely to receive compensation — but only 1,200 of 8,500 have complained
FSCS does not cover mortgage advice in the same way as deposits — customers may not be fully protected
The £45,000 average shortfall is large — compensation from FOS/redress should theoretically cover this
7,300 customers have not complained — many may not be aware of their rights
MoneyHelper / free debt advice could help customers understand their options
FCA Consumer Duty in force going forward — but this was historic advice
Conclusion: framework provides reasonable protection for those who engage with it; significant gap for non-complainants; retrospective regulation has limits

level_descriptors.descriptor: Isolated points about FCA or FSCS; little application to the case.
Identifies relevant regulatory bodies and their roles; some application to the 8,500 customers; partial conclusion.
Balanced evaluation; uses data on complainants, shortfall and uphold rate; considers limitations; supported conclusion.

Thorough, well-developed evaluation; quantifies impact of FCA action, FOS role, FSCS limits; considers non-complainants and awareness gaps; specialist vocabulary; well-justified conclusion with trade-offs acknowledged.

scenario: The UK government has raised the State Pension age to 67 and is planning to raise it to 68 by 2039. Auto-enrolment into workplace pensions is mandatory for workers aged 22+. [Table: State Pension (2025) £221.20/week; Median private sector pension pot at age 55: £37,000; Auto-enrolment minimum contributions: employee 5%, employer 3%; % of workers with adequate pension savings: 41%; Life expectancy at 65: male 83, female 85]
question: Evaluate how effectively current government pension policy prepares UK workers for retirement. (12)

indicative_content: State Pension at £221.20/week = ~£11,500/year — below average wage; insufficient alone for comfortable retirement
Median pension pot £37,000 at 55 is very low — would provide small annual income for 20-year retirement
Auto-enrolment: positive step — 8% total contribution is a start; but minimum contributions likely insufficient for full retirement income
59% of workers have inadequate savings — major gap in the system
Life expectancy of 83–85 means 18–20 years of retirement to fund — State Pension starts at 67
Raising pension age to 68 reduces pension years but saves government money
Low earners (below auto-enrolment earnings threshold) not included in auto-enrolment
Conclusion: policy takes positive steps but median pension pot and low State Pension mean many will face income shortfalls; more needs to be done to encourage higher voluntary contributions

level_descriptors.descriptor: Describes State Pension or auto-enrolment in isolation; minimal use of data.
Uses some data to compare policy features; identifies gaps; partial conclusion.
Balanced evaluation using multiple data points; considers State Pension adequacy, auto-enrolment effectiveness, and life expectancy; supported conclusion.

Thorough, well-developed evaluation; uses all key data; considers coverage gaps, income shortfalls, adequacy of contributions; specialist vocabulary; clear, justified conclusion about overall effectiveness with recommendations.

scenario: PaydayFirst is the UK's largest short-term lender. The FCA is considering three interventions: A) Imposing a total cost cap (interest + fees cannot exceed 100% of the original loan); B) Banning continuous payment authorities (CPAs) that allow the lender to repeatedly attempt to take payment; C) Requiring all applicants to complete a mandatory affordability assessment. [Table: PaydayFirst annual profit: £45m; Average loan value: £280; Average default rate: 18%; % of customers who roll over loans: 30%; FCA fine ceiling: 10% of annual turnover]
question: Evaluate which FCA intervention would most effectively protect consumers who use PaydayFirst. (12)

indicative_content: Total cost cap: prevents catastrophic debt; already in place — 30% roll-over rate suggests existing cap not fully preventing rollover harm; meaningful protection for those who do default
CPA ban: prevents lenders repeatedly draining consumers' bank accounts; protects against unexpected account emptying; stops consumers being unable to pay essential bills
Affordability assessment: prevents unsuitable lending at point of application; tackles root cause; but may restrict access for those who genuinely need emergency cash
18% default rate is high — suggests many customers are already unsuitable borrowers
30% rollover = debt escalation; cap would limit this; affordability assessment would reduce unsuitable lending
CPA: existing FCA rules already restrict CPAs — diminishing marginal benefit
Conclusion: affordability assessment tackles root cause but cost cap provides most direct protection against worst financial outcomes; combination likely optimal

level_descriptors.descriptor: Describes one intervention; limited analysis; no use of data.
Compares two interventions; uses some data; partial conclusion.
Balanced evaluation of all three; uses default rate, rollover data and loan value; supported conclusion.
Thorough evaluation; uses all data; considers root cause vs symptom treatment, affordability, existing regulations; specialist vocabulary; well-justified conclusion with acknowledged trade-offs.
